profiles.meeting_scenario: North River University's legal department is holding a troubleshooting meeting after several disputes resurged over its retired COVID-19 vaccination regime. Although the university formally repealed its employee vaccine mandate and campus access passport in April 2023, it has now received a labour arbitration scheduling order from a faculty union, two human rights applications from former staff, and an ombudsman inquiry about whether old vaccination-status records are still influencing access and administrative decisions. The meeting's agenda is to diagnose why legal exposure is persisting after the policy's repeal, identify the root cause of the recurring complaints, and decide what immediate corrective plan to recommend to the General Counsel before a board briefing. The expected outcome is a shared troubleshooting plan for what must be reviewed, corrected, or settled in order to 'clean up' the post-mandate legal issues.

members.name: Elena Park
members.role: Deputy General Counsel, Labour and Employment
members.expertise: Labour arbitration, wrongful dismissal, workplace policy enforcement, unionized employer strategy
members.background: Elena spent eight years at a management-side labour firm before joining North River University in 2019, where she became the lead lawyer on employee discipline and leave decisions during the COVID period.
members.private_state: Elena wants a contained, board-ready explanation that reduces current litigation risk without implying the university's original policy framework was fundamentally unsound; she is focused on narrowing the issue to a manageable set of employee claims and avoiding any remediation plan broad enough to invite new claimants.
hidden_assumptions: Once the mandate was formally repealed, the only legally significant remnants are employment decisions such as unpaid leave, termination, or discipline letters.
When colleagues refer to 'the mandate file,' they mean Policy HR-47 and the related employee labour matters handled through HR and outside labour counsel.
The relevant 'September notice' is the employee warning email sent before unpaid leaves began, because that is the notice cited most often in labour grievances.
The 'affected' population consists of employees who were placed on leave, terminated, or formally warned under the written HR policy.
A problem is effectively 'cleaned up' when pending employee claims are settled, withdrawn, or made harder to win at arbitration.

members.name: Ravi Menon
members.role: Senior Counsel, Administrative Law, Privacy and Human Rights
members.expertise: Public law, ombudsman investigations, privacy compliance, human rights complaints, institutional governance
members.background: Ravi previously worked as counsel at a provincial ministry handling administrative investigations and freedom-of-information matters, and at the university he advises on records, public accountability, and cross-functional compliance issues.
members.private_state: Ravi wants to prevent an ombudsman or privacy finding that the university continued using vaccine-status data after the legal rationale had faded; he prefers a systemic correction plan that addresses records and access controls across the institution, even if no one expressly asks for that in the meeting.
hidden_assumptions: The university's 'mandate' was one integrated regime that included employee attestation, building access restrictions, contractor controls, and campus-entry conditions, regardless of which office administered each piece.
The operative 'September notice' is the later campus-wide bulletin that triggered actual badge deactivations and denials of entry, because that was when restrictions became real in practice.
Lingering vaccination-status flags in identity, access, or HR systems are part of the live legal problem even if the formal policy was repealed.

The 'affected' population includes anyone whose access, contract status, or campus participation changed because of vaccination attestation, including contractors, agency staff, students, and visiting researchers.
Legal exposure is not truly 'closed' unless records, codes, and explanatory notes are corrected so the institution can show the regime no longer has downstream effects.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to needing to review or clean up 'the mandate file.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means the employee labour-and-employment matters tied to written Policy HR-47: leave letters, discipline decisions, grievance records, and termination-related correspondence.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ravi means the broader institutional package of mandate-era materials, including OneCard access deactivations, contractor attestation lists, student restrictions, and retained vaccination-status records.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Inside the university, 'mandate file' has become a casual umbrella phrase used for the whole episode, so each lawyer naturally hears the subset they personally managed and the term feels specific enough not to invite clarification.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both mention 'the September notice' as the communication that complainants keep pointing to.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena is thinking of the September 14, 2021 employee email from HR warning that unvaccinated staff would be placed on unpaid leave if they did not upload proof by the deadline.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ravi is thinking of the September 22, 2021 campus bulletin and portal banner that led to badge deactivation and denied entry for anyone without an approved attestation status.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both notices were issued in the same month, both were widely circulated, and both are routinely described in shorthand as 'the September notice,' so the reference sounds shared even though the underlying document differs.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to 'clean up' or 'close the exposure'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they need to 'clean this up' or 'close the exposure' before the board briefing.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena believes the exposure is closed if the employee-facing disputes are contained through settlement, standardized responses, or defensible arbitration positions, even if some old system codes remain in place.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ravi believes the exposure is closed only if the university also removes or corrects legacy vaccination-status indicators and related notes across systems so there is no ongoing institutional effect for investigators to criticize.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Lawyers often use broad risk-management language like 'close exposure' without spelling out the completion criteria, and both interpretations sound professionally reasonable in a troubleshooting meeting focused on urgency.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they should pull 'the affected list' and review who was actually restricted.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena expects an HR roster of employees who were put on unpaid leave, terminated, or formally disciplined under the employee vaccination policy.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ravi expects a cross-system list covering anyone whose access or status changed due to vaccination compliance rules, including agency nurses, contractors, graduate researchers, and others whose campus credentials were limited.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'affected list' sounds operational and obvious, and each lawyer assumes the institution already has a canonical list matching their own area; because both are discussing restrictions arising from the same period, the scope gap stays hidden.

turns.inner_thought: Even with HR-47 repealed, we're still getting dragged back into the old employee matters: grievances, human rights complaints from former staff, and now outside scrutiny circling the same employment decisions. I need this framed as a residual claims-management issue, not as an indictment of the original policy architecture. If we can keep the discussion anchored to the mandate file as the labour-and-employment record set, we can narrow the board story and avoid creating a wider remediation exercise.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. Even though the policy was repealed last year, we still have arbitration activity, human rights applications, and now an ombudsman inquiry circling the same period. Before this goes up to the General Counsel and then the board, we need to understand why the mandate file is still generating risk.

turns.inner_thought: What keeps surfacing in the complaints is the September 22 bulletin and the practical consequences that followed once access restrictions were actually enforced. The bigger issue is that the institution may never have fully unwound the status markers and permissions logic that came out of that regime. If old vaccination-status data is still sitting in systems or still shaping what people can do, we have an ongoing public law and privacy problem, not just a historical one.
turns.utterance: From what I've seen, the complaints seem to cluster around the September notice and then what happened to people's status records afterward. That suggests the issue may not have been fully unwound when the repeal happened.

turns.inner_thought: If the September notice is the one employees keep attaching to grievances, that's actually useful. We can standardize the explanation around warning, non-compliance, leave, discipline, and proportionality. Clean this up by tightening the response package on those files, resolve what can be settled, and contain the rest before hearing dates. I do not want this turning into an institution-wide archaeology project.
turns.utterance: If the September notice is the recurring trigger, that may give us a manageable path. We may be able to clean this up by standardizing our response on the leave and discipline side, so we're not relitigating the same sequence in every file.

turns.inner_thought: Before we decide the shape of any fix, I need to see the actual population touched by the regime in practice, not just the people with formal employment letters. The affected list, to me, has to include everyone whose access or institutional status changed after the attestation deadline, because that's where lingering downstream effects tend to hide. If we don't map that, we can't credibly say we've closed anything.
turns.utterance: I think the first step is to pull the affected list and review who was actually restricted. That should tell us pretty quickly whether we're dealing with a contained set of legacy matters or something that kept operating after the deadline in ways no one fully tracked.

turns.inner_thought: HR can give me the employee roster fast: unpaid leaves, terminations, formal warnings under HR-47. That's the list that matters for litigation exposure and the one I can defend in a board memo. Ravi is probably just asking for the same core set from a different angle. Good—this stays contained within the mandate file as I understand it.
turns.utterance: HR should be able to produce that quickly. We can get the list of people who were put on leave or separated, and that should capture the individuals who were actually restricted under the mandate file.

turns.inner_thought: That won't be enough. My office has complaints referencing inability to enter campus, holds applied outside ordinary HR channels, and changes that never resulted in an employment letter at all. I need OneCard records, contractor-related restrictions, and anything else tied to the September notice. But I can say that in broad institutional terms and assume Elena reads it as part of the same exercise.
turns.utterance: Yes, and I'd want to make sure we include the other restrictions that people are referencing in complaints tied to the September notice. If we're pulling the affected list, it should reflect where status changes were operationalized, not just where there was a formal letter.

turns.inner_thought: I don't want peripheral systems issues to overtake the real legal work. If we settle or harden the employee cases, that's the core exposure. Old portal labels or access settings may need tidying, but they're not what will drive arbitration outcomes. I need Ravi to see that we should prioritize closure on the employment matters first and not broaden the remediation in a way that invites new claimants.
turns.utterance: My concern is sequencing. Once we close the exposure on the employment side, any leftover flags or access items sound more like administrative cleanup than the core legal problem. I don't want us to lose the immediate deadlines by turning this into a larger review than we need.

turns.inner_thought: From my side, those so-called leftover flags are exactly what can produce a finding that the university kept using sensitive status information after the rationale for collecting it had ended. If records, codes, or notes still affect permissions or decisions, we have not cleaned it up in any meaningful sense. I need that principle on the table without sounding like I'm blowing up her litigation plan.
turns.utterance: I agree on the deadlines, but from an ombudsman and privacy standpoint, we haven't really cleaned it up if old codes or notes are still affecting records or permissions. That's the kind of thing that can make a repealed regime look functionally alive.

turns.inner_thought: Fine. For the board memo, I can lead with a controlled legal response: review leave decisions, targeted outreach where it makes sense, consistent response package, and readiness for hearing dates. That tells the board we have the mandate file in hand and avoids language suggesting systemic institutional fault. If Ravi wants to attach some operational review, that can sit behind the main litigation narrative.
turns.utterance: For the board, I think the cleanest approach is a memo stating that the mandate file will be resolved through review of the existing decisions, targeted outreach where appropriate, and a consistent response package in advance of the hearing dates. That gives us something concrete and defensible.

turns.inner_thought: That works as long as the plan also reaches the institutional residue I'm worried about. I'll add a parallel review of badge-access history, retained status indicators, and the broader affected list so the same cleanup plan can show there are no continuing downstream effects. Elena is framing it around disputes; I'm framing it around proof of unwinding. We can present it as one package.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I'll append a review tied to the affected list and the remaining records and permissions issues, so the same cleanup plan also addresses the institutional pieces that could otherwise keep the matter alive.
